title: Washing the body
hookLine: the Prophet's instructions to the women washing his daughter: water and lote leaves, the right side first, camphor at the end

cards: Women are washing a young woman's body when her father comes into the room. That's how a report in Sahih al-Bukhari begins, told by one of the women, Umm 'Atiyyah.
The father is the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and his daughter has died. He doesn't take over. He doesn't make a speech.
He gives them instructions, quiet and practical, the kind you'd give someone you trust with something precious. And when they finish, he hands them something of his own.

teach.b: Here's what he told them, in paraphrase from al-Bukhari. Wash her three times, or five, or more if you see the need, with water and sidr, the leaves of the lote tree. Put camphor in the last washing.

teach.h: THE RIGHT SIDE AND THE PLACES OF WUDU.
teach.b: Begin with her right side, and with the places washed in wudu. Then tell me when you've finished. Notice the tenderness in it.
The order follows the washing a person does before prayer, and some readers hear in it a last preparation, as if to stand before Allah. The lote leaves and the camphor bring cleanness and fragrance.
And the count is left open, as many times as care requires.
When they finished and told him, Umm 'Atiyyah says, he gave them his own waist-wrap and told them to wrap her in it, next to her body. A father's garment, the last thing she wore against her skin.

That's the root of a practice that continues. The washing is called ghusl. It's done by family, or by people from the community who have learned how, usually people of the same sex as the one who died.
The body is kept covered while it's washed, and handled slowly, gently, as if the person could still feel it. Some who do this work describe it as an honor.
The person on the table can't thank them, can't return the favor, can't even know, and some say that's part of what makes it pure. Dignity, here, isn't something the dead have to earn.

how: After a death, Muslims wash the body (ghusl), usually by family members or trained community volunteers of the same sex, keeping it covered, washing an odd number of times with water and often lote leaves, and adding camphor at the end.

o: the wudu that mourners make before standing for the funeral prayer
a ritual bath for the family on the day after the burial
ghusl for the one who died: water, lote leaves, gently, covered

games.q: washing the body — tap the pairs.
p: the leaves of the lote tree

s: in the report, the Prophet set a fixed number of washings
three, or five, or more if they saw the need.
he told them to begin with the right side and the places of wudu
the body is uncovered while it's washed
it's kept covered, and handled gently.

games.q: you're one of the women washing the Prophet's daughter. where does he tell you to begin?
o: with her right side and the places of wudu.
games.why: in al-Bukhari: begin with her right side and the places washed in wudu, as if preparing her for prayer.

practice: This may be tender, so go gently. Think of someone you've lost, or of the people who care for the dead in any community, and picture careful hands, a covered body, water poured slowly; notice the respect in it.
If you pray, remember those who have died. And if grief ever feels like too much to carry, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or call local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Washing the body. Ghusl for the one who has died: water and lote leaves, the right side first, camphor last, and the body kept covered and handled gently. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: washing, the full washing of the body.

carryVoice: Your line: washed with care. Gentle hands, for someone who can't say thank you. Thank you for staying with a tender day.
